questions.question: Explain how unequal heating builds the global circulation — pressure belts, cells and winds — and use the model to account for southern Africa's opposite rain seasons.
questions.expected_answer: The spherical earth receives vertical, concentrated rays in the tropics and low-angle, spread rays at the poles, creating an energy surplus equatorward of about 40 degrees and a deficit poleward, swung north and south through the year by the 23 and a half degree axial tilt. The atmosphere responds through the temperature-pressure-wind chain: heated air rises leaving the equatorial low; that air subsides near 30 degrees as the subtropical highs; subpolar lows near 60 degrees and polar highs complete the belts, all migrating with the overhead sun. The Hadley cell returns subsided air to the equator as the trade winds, the Ferrel cell drives the mid-latitude westerlies, and the polar cell sends easterlies off the ice — every wind bent left in the southern hemisphere by the Coriolis force, so the trades arrive from the south-east and the Cape's storm winds from the south-west. Southern Africa's seasons follow from the migration: in summer the ITCZ — the rising seam where the two hemispheres' trades converge — dips south and delivers the interior's thunderstorm rain, while in winter it retreats north, the subsiding Kalahari High caps the plateau in dry, frosty, cloudless weather, and the north-shifted westerlies steer cold fronts onto the south-western Cape — which is why Cape Town's rain arrives precisely when Johannesburg's stops.

questions.question: Distinguish drought from desertification, set out the types and effects of drought in southern Africa, and evaluate the management of desertification.
questions.expected_answer: Drought is a temporary shortfall: rainfall significantly below what is expected for a region, so even wet regions can suffer it — unlike aridity, which is permanent. The syllabus grades drought as meteorological, the rainfall deficit itself; hydrological, when rivers, dams and groundwater run down; agricultural, when soil moisture fails crops; and socio-economic, when shortages reach livelihoods and food prices. Southern African droughts ride recognisable drivers, above all El Niño — the periodic eastern Pacific warming that typically pushes our summer rains toward failure, with La Niña the wetter opposite — and their effects cascade from failed harvests and dying herds to empty dams, collapsing rural incomes and migration to towns. Desertification is different: the long-term degradation of dryland until it behaves like desert, caused mainly by people — overgrazing beyond the veld's carrying capacity, overcultivation exhausting fertility, deforestation for fuelwood, and poor irrigation that waterlogs and salts the soil — with drought then exposing what misuse prepared, as on the Sahel and in parts of the Northern Cape and Karoo. Management mirrors the causes: matching stock to carrying capacity and rotating grazing, contour ploughing and cover crops, replanting drought-hardy trees — the Sahel's Great Green Wall at continental scale — plus support for the rural poor, since poverty drives the survival choices that degrade the land; strategies succeed where communities are involved and fail where they only fence people out.

questions.question: Show how the arrangement of rock produces South Africa's three landform families, describe the four slope elements and the main types of mass movement, and give the contour signature of a mesa, a cuesta and a granite dome.
questions.expected_answer: How the rock lies decides the landscape. Flat sedimentary strata capped by resistant dolerite erode differentially into the Karoo sequence — plateau to mesa, broad flat top wider than its height; to butte, taller than its narrow top; to conical hill once the cap is stripped. Tilted strata weather into asymmetric ridges with a gentle dip slope along the resistant layer and a steep scarp across the broken edges, named by dip angle: cuesta at gentle dips, homoclinal ridge at moderate dips, hogsback where strata stand near vertical with both slopes steep and equal. Massive structureless granite exposed from a batholith sheds curved shells by exfoliation, keeping domes like Paarl Mountain rounded, while underground rotting of jointed blocks leaves stacked core-stones as tors. The slope dissects into crest, the convex weathered top; cliff or free face of bare bedrock; talus, the straight apron of loose debris at its angle of rest; and pediment, the gently concave foot slope — with arid South African slopes evolving by parallel retreat, the cliff eating back while the pediment widens. Mass movement, the gravity-driven downslope transfer, grades by speed and water: imperceptible soil creep shown by leaning posts and curved trunks; wet earthflows and fast deadly mudflows; landslides along straight planes and slumps rotating on curved ones leaving crescent scars; and free-falling rockfall feeding the talus — primed by steepness, water, undercutting and stripped vegetation. On the map, a mesa reads as crowded contours ringing an empty flat top with a widening skirt; a cuesta as one-sided asymmetry, packed on the scarp and spread down the dip; and a granite dome as smooth, concentric, evenly rounded rings.
